title: The Impact of Generative AI & Driving Innovation within the Court System — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source does not address whether AI automation undermines associate apprenticeship or creates a verification-expertise paradox. It redirects attention to court-service innovation, arguing that adoption depends chiefly on institutional leadership and access to technical talent.
qs: I would say the difference between a court that's leaning into innovation around this technology and one that isn't is usually a single person — a leader, either a court administrator or a chief judge or chief justice — who views this technology as an opportunity to do more or do better than the alternative.

st.t: Dispute resolution: Assistance differs from machine adjudication
st.an: The excerpt only introduces generative AI’s impact on courts as a broad topic and establishes McCormack’s relevant experience. It does not address AI-assisted versus autonomous adjudication, process redesign, safeguards, legitimacy, access outcomes, or the evidentiary basis for efficiency and reliability claims.
qs: We are your hosts, Bridget McCormick and Jen Leonard, and we are thrilled today to be talking about a really vital issue: how does generative AI impact the court system?
I'm sure we'll come back to it, because there's no way you can cover all of the things happening in courts in one episode.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source accepts that AI could expand courts’ public service while treating current initiatives as rare experiments rather than demonstrated access gains. It materially extends the cluster by identifying committed institutional leadership and technical talent as practical conditions for converting AI capability into service transformation.
qs: I would say the difference between a court that's leaning into innovation around this technology and one that isn't is usually a single person — a leader, either a court administrator or a chief judge or chief justice — who views this technology as an opportunity to do more or do better than the alternative.
Jen Leonard: I think it's so interesting because, as you mentioned, one of the challenges right now for everybody is finding talent on the technology side to help figure out how to use this well.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts managed, human-accountable adoption rather than blanket prohibition and materially extends the synthesis into court governance: existing professional duties should govern filing accuracy, while effective deployment depends on institutional training, technical capacity, proportionate rulemaking and participation by self-represented litigants.
qs: It was like, "If you use AI, you have to check everything in it" — which, you know, for anything you file with a court, you already have ethical obligations to make sure it's accurate.
They're also unsure where they're going to get the training or the technologists to help them.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source endorses court AI as a potential response to resource constraints and unmet public needs while treating current experiments as preliminary, emphasizing persistent reliability limits, institutional capacity, and inclusive public rulemaking. Its optimism is therefore bounded rather than evidence of demonstrated justice outcomes, consistent with the cluster’s comparative and risk-sensitive framing.
qs: In some ways, I think this technology is really exciting for courts because of the ways it can help them build tools and services that are really hard to create with human resources given their budgets and other constraints.
I thought the RAG process cut down on — well, it does cut down on hallucinations — but the point is, with this technology, it doesn’t eliminate them.

st.t: General platforms: Legal procedure may defend specialists
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s cautious view: Claude can improve preparation for professional legal advice, but the reported benefit is anecdotal and the speaker retains responsibility for verification and consultation with a lawyer. It does not address whether general platforms will displace specialist legal software.
qs: It made the conversation far more sophisticated and efficient than it otherwise would have been.
Obviously, I'm not relying on it entirely — you know, I understand I have to actually do the work and make sure it's correct — but I had a sort of wonky immigration/tax/employment question.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core framing that existing duties already require verified and accurate filings while AI-specific certifications and restrictions may be redundant, difficult to enforce and inconsistently designed. Its criticism of bans on self-represented litigants also aligns with bounded adoption rather than blanket prohibition, though it does not materially address sanctions doctrine.
qs: lawyers resisted the rule, in part arguing that the existing rules on the books (both the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and the rules of professional conduct that govern lawyers) already provide a structure to ensure that filings are verified, accurate, and honest.
Also, some courts say self-represented litigants can't use it, which is crazy.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source endorses leadership-enabled experimentation, coordinated judicial education and cross-institutional implementation rather than waiting for technical certainty. It also aligns with the cluster’s safeguards by acknowledging persistent hallucinations and presenting court-service and access-to-justice benefits as cautious possibilities, not demonstrated outcomes.
qs: Jen Leonard: Yeah, when somebody in power tells you it's okay to experiment and try, that really drives change.
I thought the RAG process cut down on — well, it does cut down on hallucinations — but the point is, with this technology, it doesn’t eliminate them.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source supports the engagement-first proposition by advocating resource-backed institutional collaboration to help court leaders and by highlighting judicial experimentation with generative AI. Its contribution is aspirational rather than evidentiary: it identifies participation and experimentation but provides no implementation details, safeguards or outcomes.
qs: With Thomson Reuters' resources and the National Center for State Courts' resources, we can move quickly, I hope, to put some things together to help court leaders around the country.
We'll talk in a future episode about how some judges are experimenting with using generative AI directly in their rulings and opinions, and the various reactions to that.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s framing of legal AI as organisational and public-service redesign rather than a software purchase. It attributes uneven adoption to leadership, training, technical capacity and resource constraints; advocates cross-institutional collaboration and experimentation; and treats expanded court services as promising but not yet demonstrated, with reliability limits still requiring caution.
qs: I would say the difference between a court that's leaning into innovation around this technology and one that isn't is usually a single person — a leader, either a court administrator or a chief judge or chief justice — who views this technology as an opportunity to do more or do better than the alternative.
I think there was just a lack of resources, a lack of education, a lack of information.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s supervised-use and human-accountability framing: AI-assisted filings must remain accurate and verified. It also aligns with the cluster’s account of regulatory disagreement by presenting the Fifth Circuit’s generic AI-specific certification as duplicative of existing duties and difficult to apply consistently, rather than rejecting verification itself.
qs: lawyers resisted the rule, in part arguing that the existing rules on the books (both the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and the rules of professional conduct that govern lawyers) already provide a structure to ensure that filings are verified, accurate, and honest.

They also raised issues about how a court could ever determine when something was written using AI — not to mention the fact that we use AI all the time (traditional AI) in our research products and writing tools.

kp.k: AI preparation can reduce clients' paid lawyer time
kp.d: McCormack describes using Claude to learn the basics of an unfamiliar immigration, tax and employment issue before consulting a lawyer. She reports better questions and a more efficient consultation, explicitly retaining lawyer involvement and responsibility for checking accuracy. This is a personal example rather than measured evidence of cost savings.
qs: I was going to be talking to a lawyer, but I wanted to use that time efficiently (because I wanted to pay for fewer lawyer minutes).
It gave me exactly the right questions to ask. It made the conversation far more sophisticated and efficient than it otherwise would have been.
Obviously, I'm not relying on it entirely — you know, I understand I have to actually do the work and make sure it's correct

kp.k: Drafting and factual research benefit from human verification
kp.d: Leonard reports using Claude for a first draft of a simple, low-value professional services agreement, then making adjustments. She used Perplexity to locate the counterparty's principal place of business and verified it against linked public documents. Her reported time savings are anecdotal; the workflow combines generation with human revision and source checking.
qs: I gave it some context, told the AI what the sort of scope of services was, and it generated a great first draft for me. I made a couple of adjustments.
So I was able to click on the links and verify through public documents that it was the correct principal place of business.
You can actually click on the source material, like you said, versus just relying on the text output.

kp.k: RAG supplies domain material without eliminating hallucinations
kp.d: McCormack describes retrieval augmented generation as supplementing a model with relevant data and says Clause Builder AI uses clauses upheld by courts. She is uncertain about its underlying model and characterizes RAG as a training process. She argues that it reduces rather than eliminates hallucinations. Separately, her HR chatbot example traced an incorrect answer to incorrect handbook content, illustrating the source-data problem she encountered rather than a demonstrated fabricated answer.
qs: RAG stands for "retrieval augmented generation."
we gave it an extra set of training data, which was a set of perfected clauses that have been upheld by courts.
we pulled up our HR handbook — and we had the wrong information in the HR handbook.
I thought the RAG process cut down on — well, it does cut down on hallucinations — but the point is, with this technology, it doesn’t eliminate them.

kp.k: Task selection should reflect generative AI's precision limitations
kp.d: Leonard argues that probabilistic generation can disappoint on precision-oriented tasks, including extracting direct quotations. Both speakers favor brainstorming, strategic planning and creative collaboration over treating models as document-search substitutes. These are their contemporaneous judgments about useful applications and limitations, not results from a benchmark.
qs: If people use it for some sort of really, really precision-oriented activity, the probabilistic nature of it means they'll often have disappointing outcomes. It will miss things or it will hallucinate.
That’s right. And it’s also why I think you and I have found it to be really useful for things like brainstorming and strategic planning and creative thought partnership.
But using it as sort of an upgraded version of “Control-F” to pull things out of documents — that’s much more difficult for it right now.

kp.k: Court opportunities coexist with resource and training constraints
kp.d: Drawing on presentations to judges and court administrators across multiple states, McCormack sees potential to build services that existing court budgets and staffing cannot support. She also reports anxiety about keeping pace and obtaining training and technical assistance, including one unnamed state's court technology leader who had not experimented with the technology. These are practitioner observations without a specified sample size.
qs: this technology is really exciting for courts because of the ways it can help them build tools and services that are really hard to create with human resources given their budgets and other constraints.
They're also unsure where they're going to get the training or the technologists to help them.
They had their engineering lead there, and even their chief technology officer had not had any experimentation with the technology.

kp.k: Court experiments target assistance, redesign and clerk capabilities
kp.d: McCormack reports Maricopa County building chatbots for self-represented litigants, LA County court administrator David Slayton collaborating with a Stanford team on court redesign, and Michigan's current chief justice recruiting three incoming clerks eager to experiment with generative AI. She presents these as rare examples of innovation; the claimed scaling of public assistance is an anticipated benefit, not an evaluated outcome.
qs: the Maricopa County court is building chatbots for self-represented litigants using this technology
There's now an unlimited number of AI assistants that can answer them, right?
There's David Slayton, who's a court administrator in LA County, partnering with a team at Stanford to try to figure out how to redesign what courts should be for the public who needs them.
she’s hiring new clerks, three new clerks coming in, and she specifically hired people who were eager to play with generative AI tools and technology to improve the work of the courts.

kp.d: McCormack attributes differences in court innovation largely to individual leaders who see an opportunity to improve services, contrasting this with lawyers' skepticism and risk aversion. Leonard reports analogous differences in law firms and law schools and argues that leaders' permission to experiment spreads through organizations. Their account proposes a leadership mechanism rather than demonstrating causation.
qs: I would say the difference between a court that's leaning into innovation around this technology and one that isn't is usually a single person — a leader, either a court administrator or a chief judge or chief justice — who views this technology as an opportunity to do more or do better than the alternative.
judges are lawyers, and lawyers are skeptical by nature and risk-averse by training.
when somebody in power tells you it's okay to experiment and try, that really drives change.

kp.k: Fifth Circuit withdrawal favors existing accuracy obligations
kp.d: Leonard describes a proposed Fifth Circuit certification rule for generative-AI-assisted filings and its withdrawal following objections about redundant accuracy obligations and identifying AI use. McCormack endorses that interpretation, highlighting Louisiana appellate judge Scott Schlegel's comment and treating the episode as successful public rulemaking and a metaphor for professional adaptation. The discussion reports a withdrawn proposal, not a continuing requirement.
qs: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit (a federal appellate court) recently proposed a rule that would have required attorneys to certify the accuracy of any legal filings involving the use of generative AI.
They also raised issues about how a court could ever determine when something was written using AI
for anything you file with a court, you already have ethical obligations to make sure it's accurate. Those obligations already exist.
The public basically said, "You know what, we already have rules that require us to do this, so this is not a good idea," and the court withdrew the rule.

kp.k: Fragmented court restrictions can impede self-represented litigants
kp.d: McCormack reports heterogeneous AI orders, including outright bans and restrictions on pro hac vice lawyers or self-represented litigants, and strongly opposes the latter. Leonard reports counting 52 orders on Duke Law's RAILS website on the day of the conversation. McCormack identifies an unresolved information gap about how many original orders have subsequently been amended or rescinded.
qs: We've seen lots of court orders — some early ones that were pretty aggressive about banning all use of generative AI by lawyers in proceedings, and then some more nuanced ones.
Also, some courts say self-represented litigants can't use it, which is crazy.
Well, I logged onto RAILS today and by my most recent count there are 52 orders from different courts about AI usage.
What I want to know — and I can't find this online right now — is how many of those orders that were issued originally have been amended or rescinded.

kp.k: Public outreach is necessary for inclusive court rulemaking
kp.d: Leonard contrasts lawyers' ability to participate in rulemaking with the need to protect self-represented litigants' access to AI. McCormack argues that merely posting proposals on court websites fails to reach people whose access to justice may be affected. She cites organized outreach around post-pandemic remote-hearing rules as an example of obtaining public views beyond those of lawyers and judges.
qs: some rules can keep you out of court or let you in.
I don't think most members of the public who might have a justice problem are perusing court websites to see if there's some potential rule change that might impact their ability to get justice.
legal services organizations or organizations that work on materials for self-represented litigants helped get the information out to the public so they could be heard on an issue that impacts them.
Lawyers had one view; judges had a very strong view in one direction. But really it's the public that you want to hear from, right?

kp.k: New partnership seeks judicial education and access improvements
kp.d: Leonard describes a National Center for State Courts–Thomson Reuters Institute partnership focused on judicial AI education, informed decisions, access to justice and policy responses protecting the rule of law. McCormack reports council membership and chairing its access-to-justice workstream, with only one meeting held so far. Her expectation that pooled resources and cross-disciplinary collaboration could produce new services and support courts quickly is explicitly prospective.
qs: The goals of the partnership are to inform and educate the judiciary about all the opportunities and challenges created by AI, to help judges make informed decisions, to expand access to justice, and to develop policy responses so that we protect the rule of law from some of the potential challenges.
I'm actually on this council — we've had one meeting so far — and they have me chairing the access to justice workstream.
With Thomson Reuters' resources and the National Center for State Courts' resources, we can move quickly, I hope, to put some things together to help court leaders around the country.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: McCormack says general-purpose generative AI can help clients understand unfamiliar legal frameworks and make consultations with lawyers more efficient.
pts.d: McCormack describes using Claude to prepare for a lawyer consultation involving immigration, tax and employment issues. She reports better questions and a more sophisticated, efficient conversation; paying for fewer lawyer minutes was her objective, not a quantified outcome. This is an account of AI-assisted preparation, not a claim that AI replaces legal advice. She explicitly retains checking and consultation with a lawyer.

pts.k: Leonard reports that AI accelerates simple agreement drafting and ancillary fact-finding, with human adjustment and source verification.
pts.d: Speaking about her own work rather than introducing someone else's claim, Leonard describes Claude producing a first draft of a simple, low-value professional services agreement. She adjusted the draft and used Perplexity to find the counterparty's principal place of business, then checked linked public documents. Her claimed time savings are experiential and approximate, not measured. McCormack separately reports that Perplexity has largely displaced Google in her own searching.

pts.k: The speakers describe task-dependent usefulness: current models are useful for drafting and ideation but unreliable for precision-dependent extraction; retrieval and source links do not remove the need to check outputs.
pts.d: Leonard attributes missed information and hallucinations to probabilistic generation and says brainstorming, strategic planning and creative partnership are more useful applications for her than exact quotation retrieval. McCormack describes Clause Builder AI drawing on a collection of clauses upheld by courts, and claims RAG reduces but does not eliminate hallucinations. Her accompanying HR-chatbot anecdote concerns incorrect information already present in a handbook, rather than demonstrating fabricated output. No measured reliability rate is supplied. The speakers call RAG a training process; that is their characterization of the implementation, not evidence of model retraining.

pts.k: McCormack predicts that generative AI can expand court services beyond what constrained human staffing and budgets allow, particularly assistance for self-represented litigants.
pts.d: McCormack cites Maricopa County's development of chatbots as a concrete example of potential expansion in public-facing assistance. She contrasts a small number of human question-answerers with what she describes as an unlimited number of AI assistants. The transcript establishes an initiative under development and her expectation of scalable service, not measured improvements in access, accuracy or case outcomes.

pts.k: McCormack says court adoption is constrained by limited expertise and resources and is often driven by an individual leader willing to experiment.
pts.d: Drawing on presentations to judges and court administrators in multiple states, McCormack reports concern about disrupted processes, increased demands and access to training or technologists. She says innovative exceptions are rare and usually associated with a chief judge, chief justice or administrator. Examples include the Los Angeles County court administrator's Stanford collaboration and Michigan's chief justice hiring three clerks eager to experiment with AI. Leonard contributes her own observations of similar leadership differences in law firms and law schools. These are qualitative observations, not a causal study.

pts.k: McCormack interprets the Fifth Circuit's withdrawal of a proposed AI certification rule as movement from defensive restrictions toward relying on existing accuracy obligations.
pts.d: McCormack endorses the argument that lawyers already must ensure the accuracy of court filings, irrespective of the tools used. She describes the Fifth Circuit proposal and public comments as an example of the profession's uneven adaptation to AI, rather than proof of a uniform regulatory trend. She also reports varied restrictions across courts, including bans affecting pro hac vice lawyers and self-represented litigants. Leonard reports counting 52 court AI orders on Duke's RAILS site that day. McCormack explicitly says she does not know how many earlier orders have subsequently been amended or rescinded.

pts.k: McCormack expects cross-organizational collaboration to help courts develop AI-enabled access-to-justice services, but presents this as an early-stage possibility.
pts.d: McCormack describes the National Center for State Courts–Thomson Reuters Institute partnership as promising for judicial support and access to justice. As a council member chairing the access-to-justice workstream, she hopes pooled resources and creative collaboration can produce new products, services and ways of working quickly. The council had held only one meeting; the transcript supplies no completed outputs, adoption metrics or demonstrated justice outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies primarily on personal use, professional experience, named initiatives and a rulemaking example, rather than quantitative tests of AI's effects.
pts.d: The efficiency claims rest on McCormack's and Leonard's own recent use. Court-adoption claims rest on McCormack's judicial background and presentations across states, with Maricopa County, Los Angeles County and Michigan offered as examples. The Fifth Circuit discussion supplies a specific institutional episode, and Leonard's 52-order count describes regulatory activity, not AI performance. Clause Builder and the HR chatbot supply implementation anecdotes without controlled comparisons. Partnership predictions draw on McCormack's direct participation. References to Adam Unikowsky and Ethan Mollick are secondhand context, not separately demonstrated findings in this episode. No benchmark scores, measured hallucination rates, staffing reductions or quantified access-to-justice gains are reported.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Claims concern recent experience and ongoing experimentation in 2024; future benefits have no fixed forecast horizon.
pts.d: Personal-use examples occurred in the preceding weeks. Precision limitations are explicitly qualified as applying currently or for now. Court chatbots are described as being built, innovative courts as rare, and the partnership as having held one meeting. Expected benefits depend on suitable task selection, human verification, relevant source material, resources, education and leadership permission to experiment. The series title '2030 Vision' is not a stated deadline for these claims. Potential services and faster institutional progress are expressed as hopes or possibilities rather than assured outcomes.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are courts and their users, especially self-represented litigants; lawyers and clients also face changes to preparation, drafting and verification.
pts.d: Clients may arrive better prepared and seek fewer paid consultation minutes. Lawyers and other agreement drafters may save time while remaining responsible for checking their work. Judges, administrators, clerks and court technologists face training and capacity demands as well as opportunities to redesign services. Self-represented litigants may gain scalable help but can also be excluded from using AI by court restrictions. McCormack emphasizes that ordinary court users are less likely than lawyers to participate in website-based rulemaking, making public outreach important when rules affect access. The source does not predict profession-wide job losses, specific law-firm staffing changes or market-share shifts.
